claims.text: Applying a thin, dense, nanocrystalline Al2O3 coating by atomic layer deposition will improve the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy cladding.
ALD Al2O3-coated zirconium-alloy cladding will retain suitability for service.
Standard zirconium-alloy cladding has a native, imperfect surface oxide layer.
The proposed intervention is deposition of an Al2O3 coating less than 100 nm thick by ALD.
The proposed benefit should hold in oxidizing atmospheres at 1200–1500 °C under mechanical stresses representative of reactor service.
ALD will provide a continuous, homogeneous alumina layer on the cladding surface.
The continuous alumina layer will act as a physical barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Impeded oxygen diffusion into the zirconium alloy will slow oxidation kinetics.
The alumina coating will mimic the thermal expansion of the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Thermal-expansion compatibility will allow the coating to retain adhesion and mechanical integrity.
The coating will reduce oxide-scale growth rate by at least 30–50% relative to uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding.
The coating will not cause detrimental changes in mechanical properties under service conditions.
The oxidation-resistance benefit depends on the alumina layer remaining adherent and intact during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Delamination or cracking of the coating may compromise its protective performance.
Temperatures significantly above 1600 °C or extreme mechanical stresses may compromise coating performance.
Long-term coating stability under neutron irradiation and repeated thermal cycling is uncertain.
A controlled comparison at approximately 1400 °C for 30 minutes under an oxidizing atmosphere and simulated service loads is proposed.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction of at least 30% in oxide-scale growth, or occurrence of delamination or compromised mechanical properties, will falsify the hypothesis.
